title: MCA or MHA? Capacity in mental illness
blurb: Assess capacity in mental illness and choose correctly between the Mental Capacity Act and the Mental Health Act.
question: Mr Clarke, 72, has severe depression with psychotic features. He lacks capacity to decide about admission and is clearly objecting, pushing staff away and asking to go home. The team agree hospital treatment is needed and the care plan would deprive him of his liberty. Which legal framework should be used?

teach.body: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (MCA) lets others act in the best interests of a person who lacks capacity for a specific decision. The Mental Health Act 1983 (MHA) allows detention and treatment for mental disorder, whether or not the person has capacity. In plain English: the MCA is about who decides when someone cannot; the MHA is about when the law may override someone's choice for their mental disorder.

steps.label: Presume capacity
steps.sub: s1(2); help first with all practicable steps

steps.label: Understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate?
steps.sub: Unable to do any one = unable to decide

teach.caption: An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity (s1(4)). A diagnosis alone never settles capacity.

teach.h: Options grid for hospital treatment of mental disorder (COP15 Figure 5)
teach.caption: Grid applies where the care plan amounts to a deprivation of liberty. A person cannot be under MHA detention and a DoLS authorisation at the same time.

items: Under 16: competence is judged by Gillick; the MCA does not apply below 16.
16 and 17: capacity for informal admission is judged under the MCA (s131(5)).
A capable 16- or 17-year-old's consent to informal admission is enough even if a parent disagrees (s131(3)).
A capable 16- or 17-year-old's refusal cannot be overridden by a parent's consent (s131(4)); consider the MHA.

teach.body: Capacity in mental illness often changes: a person with mania or psychosis may have capacity one day and not the next. The Code says that if a person may regain capacity or has fluctuating capacity, the MHA should be preferred over DoLS to authorise a deprivation of liberty (COP15 13.54). Whenever in doubt about whether someone objects, assume they are objecting (13.51). DoLS remain the scheme in force; the Liberty Protection Safeguards have not been implemented.

head: Scheme
Status
rows: In force: hospitals and care homes, aged 18+
teach.caption: Teach and apply DoLS and the 1983 Act as amended until new schemes are commenced.

teach.body: Mr Clarke lacks capacity about admission, and he is objecting. The objection is judged in the round, not by whether it seems reasonable. Where a person objects, the Code's grid says only the MHA is available, so DoLS and informal admission are not options. The AMHP and doctors assess him for s2 or s3. His physical health care unrelated to depression, such as treatment of a chest infection, would still need his consent or a best-interests decision under the MCA.

teach.text: Do not use the MCA to give treatment regulated by Part 4 of the MHA (MCA s28). And do not informally admit a person who lacks capacity to consent to admission where the arrangements will deprive them of liberty, even if they seem content (COP15 13.53).

items: Capacity is decision- and time-specific and can fluctuate in mental illness; presume it and support it.
Objecting (capable or not) to hospital treatment for mental disorder: the MHA is the route.
Lacks capacity and not objecting, with a deprivation of liberty: MHA or DoLS; prefer the MHA if capacity fluctuates.
MCA cannot authorise Part 4 treatment; 16-17s are covered by s131 and the MCA; DoLS, not LPS, is in force.

summary: You can now assess capacity in someone with a mental illness, recognise when it fluctuates, and use the Code's options grid to choose between the MHA, DoLS and informal admission. You can also explain s131 for 16- and 17-year-olds and the MCA s28 bar.

A.q: A patient with schizophrenia refuses an antibiotic for a chest infection. Which statement about his capacity is correct?
options: His diagnosis means he lacks capacity
He must be presumed to have capacity
Capacity is assessed by his RC alone
He lacks capacity because he refuses
A.why: MCA s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; a diagnosis cannot by itself establish incapacity (s2(3)).

whyNot.0: A condition alone cannot establish lack of capacity.
whyNot.2: The person making the decision assesses capacity, which need not be the RC.
whyNot.3: An unwise decision or refusal is not proof of incapacity (s1(4)).

A.q: Which statement about the Mental Capacity Act and treatment of a detained patient is correct?
options: The MCA can authorise s58 medication
The MCA overrides Part 4 if capacity is lacking
The MCA cannot authorise Part 4 treatment
The MCA authorises it if the RC agrees
A.why: MCA s28(1): nothing in the MCA authorises treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA.

whyNot.0: Section 58 treatment is regulated by Part 4, so the MCA cannot authorise it.
whyNot.1: Part 4 governs; the MCA does not override it.
whyNot.3: The RC's agreement does not lift the s28 bar on using the MCA for Part 4 treatment.

A.q: Under the MCA, which is one of the abilities a person must have to make a decision?
A.why: MCA s3(1): a person is unable to decide if unable to understand, retain, use or weigh the information, or communicate the decision.

whyNot.0: Agreement is not required; capable people can disagree.
whyNot.2: Communication can be by any means, not necessarily writing.
whyNot.3: Retaining information for a short period is enough (s3(3)).

B.q: Sam, 17, has capacity and agrees to informal admission to an adolescent unit. His father objects. What is the legal position?
B.why: MHA s131(3): a capable 16- or 17-year-old's consent to informal admission is sufficient even if a person with parental responsibility disagrees.

whyNot.1: A parent cannot block a capable 16- or 17-year-old's consent.
whyNot.2: Parental consent is not required when Sam has capacity and consents.
whyNot.3: No court order is required for capable consent to informal admission.

B.q: Erin, 16, has capacity and refuses admission for her eating disorder. Her mother says she will consent for her. What is the correct position?
options: Her mother's consent cannot override her refusal
She can be admitted under the MCA in her best interests
B.why: MHA s131(4): a capable 16- or 17-year-old's refusal of informal admission cannot be overridden by the consent of a person with parental responsibility. The MHA may be considered if criteria are met.

whyNot.0: Section 131(4) prevents a parent consenting over a capable refusal.
whyNot.2: For 16-17s, capacity for informal admission is judged under the MCA (s131(5)).
whyNot.3: She has capacity, so the MCA cannot authorise admission.

B.q: Mrs Webb lacks capacity to consent to admission for her psychotic illness. She seems content and is not objecting. The care plan will deprive her of her liberty. What does the Code say about informal admission?
options: It is appropriate as she is not objecting
It is acceptable with family agreement
It is acceptable for up to 28 days
It should not be used in this situation
B.why: COP15 13.53: a person who lacks capacity to consent to admission and is likely to be deprived of liberty should not be informally admitted, whether or not content. The MHA or DoLS should be used.

whyNot.0: Not objecting does not make informal admission lawful where she lacks capacity and will be deprived of liberty.
whyNot.1: Family agreement does not authorise a deprivation of liberty.
whyNot.2: No 28-day informal option exists for this situation.

C.q: Mr Clarke lacks capacity to decide about admission and is pushing staff away, asking to go home. Hospital treatment for his depression is needed and would deprive him of liberty. Which framework fits?
options: Assessment under the Mental Health Act
C.why: COP15 Figure 5: where the person objects to hospital admission or treatment for mental disorder, whether capable or not, only the MHA is available.

whyNot.0: DoLS is not available where the person objects to treatment for mental disorder in hospital.
whyNot.1: Informal admission is not appropriate for someone lacking capacity who will be deprived of liberty.
whyNot.3: The MCA cannot authorise a deprivation of liberty for an objecting patient in this situation.

C.q: Rosa, 40, with bipolar disorder, lacks capacity during manic episodes but regains it between them. She is manic now and does not object to admission. The team must authorise a deprivation of liberty. Which option does the Code prefer?
options: Informal admission based on her current consent
Detention under the Mental Health Act
C.why: COP15 13.54: where a person may regain capacity or has fluctuating capacity, use of the MHA should be preferred over DoLS or a Court of Protection order.

whyNot.0: A Court of Protection order is available but not preferred with fluctuating capacity.
whyNot.1: DoLS is available but the Code prefers the MHA where capacity fluctuates.
whyNot.2: She currently lacks capacity, so she cannot consent to informal admission.

C.q: Joe, detained under section 3 for psychosis, lacks capacity to consent to a dental extraction for a painful abscess unrelated to his mental disorder. What authorises the extraction?
options: The MCA, in his best interests
C.why: The MHA does not regulate treatment of physical conditions unrelated to mental disorder (COP15 13.32); for a person lacking capacity, the MCA best-interests framework applies.

whyNot.0: Section 63 covers treatment for mental disorder, not unrelated physical treatment.
whyNot.1: SOADs certify Part 4 treatment for mental disorder.
whyNot.3: The nearest relative cannot consent to treatment for an adult.

reteach.title: Two questions settle most cases
reteach.question: Faced with an unwell person who may need hospital, what do you ask first?

blocks.h: Is it mental disorder treatment? Do they object?
blocks.body: First: is the treatment for mental disorder, or for an unrelated physical problem? Unrelated physical treatment is consent or the MCA, even for detained patients. Second, for hospital treatment of mental disorder: does the person object? If yes, capable or not, the MHA is the route. If they lack capacity and do not object, the MHA or DoLS can be used, and the MHA is preferred when capacity fluctuates.

blocks.text: When unsure whether a person is objecting, the Code says to treat them as objecting (COP15 13.51).

explain.body: Presume capacity, give all practicable help, and assess each decision at the time it is needed. Mental illness may affect the ability to use or weigh information, especially in psychosis or mania, but a diagnosis alone does not settle it.

test.q: A patient with mania has capacity to choose his meals but not to manage large financial transfers. How is this best described?
test.why: Capacity is assessed for a specific decision at a specific time, so a person can have capacity for one decision and not another.

whyNot.1: Capacity is not an all-or-nothing status.
whyNot.2: Capacity is not an all-or-nothing status.
whyNot.3: A diagnosis alone cannot establish capacity or incapacity.

explain.body: Objecting, with or without capacity: MHA only. Capable and not objecting: informal admission or the MHA. Lacks capacity and not objecting: MHA or DoLS. Never both MHA detention and DoLS at once.

test.q: A capable patient refuses admission for mental disorder and meets the section 2 criteria. Which framework is available?
test.why: A capable person's refusal cannot be overridden under the MCA; where criteria are met, only the MHA is available.

whyNot.0: DoLS requires lack of capacity and is not available for an objecting patient.
whyNot.1: The MCA does not apply to a person with capacity.
whyNot.3: The Court of Protection acts for people who lack capacity.

explain.body: The MCA cannot be used to give treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA. It can be used for a person lacking capacity whose treatment is not regulated by Part 4, such as an informal patient, in their best interests.

test.q: An informal in-patient lacks capacity to consent to an oral antidepressant and does not resist. What can authorise it?
test.why: COP15 13.31: the MCA can be used to treat mental disorder where the person lacks capacity and the treatment is not regulated by Part 4, as for an informal patient.

whyNot.3: SOAD certificates belong to Part 4 for detained or CTO patients.

explain.body: Capacity for informal admission is judged under the MCA. Capable consent is enough despite a parent's objection; a capable refusal cannot be overridden by a parent. Under 16: Gillick competence.

test.q: Under which law is the capacity of a 16-year-old to consent to informal admission judged?
test.why: MHA s131(5): capacity of a 16- or 17-year-old for informal admission is read in accordance with the MCA.

whyNot.1: The Children Act defines parental responsibility for s131 but not capacity.
whyNot.3: Fraser guidelines concern contraceptive advice to under-16s.
